changes.before: Implement allowedOrigin(origin). Match the worked contract and the changed-input checks without modifying the supplied input values.
changes.after: An allowed website address does not prove that a user has permission to read a private note.

before: An origin combines scheme, host, and port. A browser cross-origin policy may allow selected origins to read a response, but it is not a substitute for authentication or authorization.
This exercise is a small pure JavaScript model. Its inputs are supplied directly; it does not receive live HTTP requests, operate a database, or deploy a service.

includes performs exact membership comparison in this small allowlist. A substring check could accept a lookalike host. This exercise returns a policy decision; it does not configure CORS response headers.

Read the function call allowedOrigin("https://notes.example.test") from the inside out: the arguments supply the inputs, allowedOrigin runs the body once, and return sends its result back to the caller. console.log displays that result; it does not change it.
An origin is allowed. Does that prove its user owns a private record? Origin policy governs browser access. It does not identify a particular user or grant record ownership.
after: An origin is the combination of a website's scheme, host, and port. The scheme is a prefix such as https. The host is the site name. The port tells the computer which service to reach.
CORS is a browser rule for sharing responses across origins. A server can allow selected origins to read a response. That does not prove who the user is.
includes checks whether the whole value is in the list. A similar-looking address is not the same origin. Checking only part of an address could accept the wrong site.
allowedOrigin returns true or false. console.log shows that result. This helper only makes the decision; it does not set real CORS headers.
Before returning a private note, the server must still check the user's identity and permission to read that note. An allowed origin alone cannot prove either.
